# Deploy the Terraform MCP server

The Terraform MCP server gives AI models up-to-date information from the
Terraform registry and, when connected, from your HCP Terraform or Terraform
Enterprise organizations.

You can run the Terraform Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on your local
machine, host it in an environment that you manage, or connect to the remote
Terraform MCP server that HashiCorp hosts for HCP Terraform. 

 > **Hands-on**: Try the [Integrate your private module registry with the
 > Terraform MCP server tutorial](/terraform/tutorials/cloud/mcp).
 > Learn how to use the Terraform MCP server to explore your HCP Terraform
 > private registry and generate Terraform configuration.

## Deployment options 

You can run the Terraform MCP server on your local machine, host it in a remote
environment that you manage, or connect to the remote Terraform MCP server that
HashiCorp hosts.

- Local deployments are best for helping you get started or for one-off projects. Refer to [Deploy Terraform MCP server locally](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/local) for instructions.
- Self-hosted deployments are best for centrally managing the server, which helps you implement good governance policies across your organizations. Self-hosted deployments also support Terraform Enterprise. Refer to [Deploy a self-hosted Terraform MCP server](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted) for instructions.
- The remote Terraform MCP server is best for connecting to HCP Terraform without installing or operating a server. The remote Terraform MCP server is in beta. Refer to [Connect to the remote Terraform MCP server](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/remote-mcp) for instructions.

The following table compares deployment options.

| | Local MCP | Self-hosted MCP | Remote MCP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who runs the server | You, on your machine | You, in an environment you manage | HashiCorp |
| Transport | `stdio` or `streamable-http` | `streamable-http` | `streamable-http` |
| Installation | Docker, binary, or source | Docker, binary, or source | None |
| HCP Terraform | Supported | Supported | Supported, requires an API token |
| Terraform Enterprise | Supported | Supported | Not supported |
| Server configuration | You control it | You control it | HashiCorp controls it |

## Secure configuration

Implement the following recommendations to securely deploy a local or
self-hosted MCP server: 

- Hosting
  
  We recommend running your MCP server locally at `127.0.0.1` through [the STDIO or HTTP Streamable transport protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/transports) to limit publicly exposing your Terraform environment. The default transport is set to STDIO. If you host your server remotely, we recommend implementing additional security controls at the application and network layers. For example, you can add an API gateway with authentication, TLS encryption, and IP whitelisting between the client and server.
- CORS

  By default, Terraform MCP server runs in `strict` [CORS (cross-origin request)](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-cors-protocol) mode and the allowed origins are empty. As a result, all cross-origin requests are blocked unless the server is explicitly configured to allow them. Exercise caution when changing the allowed origins list.
- Terraform authentication

  The `TFE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY` option is set to `false` by default so that the MCP server verifies that the HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise TLS certificate is valid. If you temporarily set this option to `true` for testing or other use cases, we strongly recommend resetting to `false` to ensure that encryption is enabled. We also recommend limiting the permissions of the `TFE_TOKEN` used to authenticate as described in the Terraform documentation. Refer to [API tokens](/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/api-tokens) for more information.
- Rate limiting

  We recommend setting up global and per-session rate limits to prevent the server or dependent resources from becoming overloaded through excessive requests. 
- TLS

  When making your MCP server accessible remotely, we recommend adding TLS certificates to the host infrastructure to protect in-transit communication. To serve HTTPS from the server itself, set the `MCP_TLS_CERT_FILE` and `MCP_TLS_KEY_FILE` environment variables. Refer to [Configure TLS](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted#configure-tls) for more information.
- Organization allowlist

  When you host your server remotely, we recommend
  restricting access to the organizations that you expect to use the server.
  Refer to [Restrict access by
  organization](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/self-hosted#restrict-access-by-organization)
  for more information.

HashiCorp manages the configuration of the remote
Terraform MCP server. Refer to [remote Terraform MCP server
security](/terraform/mcp-server/security#remote-terraform-mcp-server-security)
for more information.

## Authentication

You must use Terraform MCP server v0.3.0 or newer to authenticate with the
Terraform registry. Authentication requires an authentication token
from HCP Terraform or your Terraform Enterprise deployment so that the MCP
server can access your private registry. Refer to [API
tokens](/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/api-tokens) for
instructions.

We recommend authenticating the server with HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise so that you can interact with your organization and private registry. Refer to [Connect to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/local#connect-to-hcp-terraform-or-terraform-enterprise) for more information.

The remote Terraform MCP server requires an HCP Terraform user or team API token
for every request. Refer to [Create an API
token](/terraform/mcp-server/deploy/remote-mcp#create-an-api-token) for more
information.
